lines.text: Vera, does the model read my words?
Not words, not letters. Numbered pieces from a fixed list.
Numbered pieces? Like me?
Like you. Each piece is a token, and the model only sees its number.
Why not just use letters?
The list stays tiny, but every sentence gets very long.
One number per word, then?
Then the list explodes, and any new word is simply unknown.
So what's in between?
Byte-pair encoding. Start from characters, and keep gluing the most frequent neighbouring pair.
lines.say: Byte pair encoding. Start from characters, and keep gluing the most frequent neighbouring pair.

lines.text: So common words end up as one piece?
Right. Here, “learned” is one token, but “unbelievably” stays in pieces.
lines.say: Right. Here, learned is one token, but unbelievably stays in pieces.

lines.text: Real models use lists of about 50,000 to 200,000 pieces.
lines.say: Real models use lists of about fifty thousand to two hundred thousand pieces.

lines.text: Why should I care?
Prices, context limits and speed are all counted in tokens, not words.
In English, a token is about four characters on average.
And in Hebrew?
Languages rarer in the training text, like Hebrew, need more tokens for the same meaning.
So the same message costs more and fits less.
Then how many r's are in “strawberry”?
lines.say: Then how many R's are in strawberry?

lines.text: Three. But a chatbot may miscount: it never sees letters, only chunks like str, aw, berry.
lines.say: Three. But a chatbot may miscount: it never sees letters, only chunks, like S T R, A W, berry.

lines.text: So the r's are hidden inside the chunks.
lines.say: So the R's are hidden inside the chunks.

lines.text: Exactly. Sums with long numbers trip up the same way.
Can I chop some text myself?
Slide the merges in the Tokens chapter, or play Chop Shop in the game.
Eight glues, fewest packets? I'm in.
